subject: Washington reshuffles its 50% tariff list on Canada
bodyMarkdown:
If you know someone in Ontario who makes carpet or paint and sells it into the United States, their landed cost changes on Friday. Donald Trump signed a proclamation last Friday rewriting which Canadian goods face 50 per cent American duties, and the new list takes effect October 30.

## What actually changed on Friday

The duties run through **Section 338**, a clause of the 1930 Tariff Act that lets a president add duties on a country he says discriminates against American commerce. The White House fact sheet on the proclamation says plywood sheets, some paper products, certain machinery and refrigeration equipment, and certain packing crates and boxes come out of the 50 per cent band. Going in are carpets and floor coverings, certain valves, cocoa powders, paints, shampoos, archery equipment, waste products and canoes. CNBC reported on October 20 that these duties cover roughly US$20 billion of Canadian exports, about five per cent of what we sell south, and that they took effect August 22. The detail exporters keep getting wrong is that they apply whether or not a good qualifies under CUSMA. Ottawa answered in September with counter-tariffs on C$27.6 billion of American imports, at rates of 15, 25 and 50 per cent.

## Why the timing looks political to me

Americans vote on November 3. A writer at Reason's Volokh Conspiracy argued on October 25 that the exemptions are probably meant to help Senator Susan Collins of Maine and other congressional Republicans who fear a backlash at the polls, and I find that reading hard to avoid. Maine buys Canadian paper and lumber. Plywood and paper came off the list. The White House frames the change as a public interest adjustment meant to make the measures work better, and both of those can be true at once. What matters if you run a business is that this list moves with the American political calendar, so it can be turned again in either direction before Christmas. If your product came off on Friday, I would not rebuild next year's pricing around it.

## The lawsuit that could erase all of it

On October 20 a food importer, Gellert Global Group, sued at the U.S. Court of International Trade, represented by the Liberty Justice Center. CNBC covered the filing that day. The complaint asks the court to declare the Section 338 duties unlawful, stop their collection, and order refunds with interest, for the company and a proposed class of other importers. Its central argument is that later trade legislation impliedly repealed the 1930 provision, so the authority being used no longer exists. Reporting on the case noted that the Supreme Court has already struck down the emergency powers tariffs, and that the Court of International Trade ruled against the Section 122 measures brought in to replace them, a decision now on appeal. No ruling on this one yet.

## The takeaway

Pull your HS codes and check them against the new list before Friday rather than after, because the duty lands at the border whether or not the good is CUSMA qualifying. Ottawa's CUSMA consultation closes November 3, the same day Americans vote, and a short submission from a small exporter counts for more than silence, so write one. I am watching the Court of International Trade docket more closely than the product list, since a ruling there would reach every line on it at once. If your product did come off on Friday, treat the relief as something with an expiry date.
